question: You inherit a pattern-recognition service built on a Rosenblatt-style perceptron: retina S-points feed randomly wired A-units, and only the A→R stage is trained, by reinforcing the value V of A-units that were active when a response was rewarded. Product asks for two things: an audit trail naming which unit holds the "cat" pattern so it can be deleted on request, and a guarantee that deleting it leaves the other learned classes untouched. What does the architecture say?
choices: Neither is available, and that follows from the design premise rather than from an implementation shortcut. The connectionist bet is that a stimulus is stored as strengthened connections rather than as a coded record, so recognition needs no lookup and there is no entry to excise; memory is distributed, and removing part of the association layer degrades every learned response a little and none of them completely. Supplying the audit trail means replacing the architecture, not instrumenting it

Both are straightforward from the training signal itself: log which A-units were active during each reinforcement of "cat", and that active set is the record — zeroing the value of those units deletes the class cleanly while other responses, which were reinforced on their own passes, keep the values they earned

The random S→A wiring is the only obstacle. Replace the scattered origin points with a designed encoding of one interpretable feature per A-unit, and both requirements fall out — each class becomes identifiable by the named features that support it, with the A→R learning rule left exactly as it is

Both become available once training has converged, because V only ever increases under reinforcement: the highest-valued A-units in a response's source-set are that response's record by construction, so resetting the top of that ranking removes the class and leaves lower-valued units, which belong to other responses, undisturbed
explanation: The judgment being tested is recognising when a product requirement is asking a design premise to be false. Rosenblatt's starting position is not an algorithm but a claim about where information lives: as new connections rather than as coded records, which is exactly why a recognising system needs no separate lookup stage — the strengthened pathways simply fire. Distributed memory is the direct consequence, and Rosenblatt names it as a conclusion: damage to part of the association layer degrades everything a little and nothing completely. That property is inseparable from the storage scheme; you cannot keep the storage and add per-class localisation on top. The second option is the most tempting because its first half is true — active units that fire under reinforcement do gain value, so the active set is real and loggable. What breaks is the assumption of exclusivity: an A-unit fires on whatever stimuli its random source-set happens to overlap, so the same units accumulate value across many classes, and zeroing them removes evidence for responses nobody asked to delete. That is graceful degradation seen from the other side. The third option misplaces the distribution. Designing the first layer changes where the features come from, not how they are combined: the R-units are still fed by source-sets of A-units, still with learning spread across many connections, so no class gets a single home. It is also the wrong reading of why the wiring is random — the scattered origin points are a modelling commitment, treating imperfect and largely random nervous tissue with probability theory rather than the exact-wiring symbolic logic of McCulloch and Pitts, and that first layer is wiring, not learning. The fourth option turns a ranking into a record. High value marks a unit as useful to a response, not as owned by it, and "useful to this response" and "useful to another" are not mutually exclusive states of the same unit.

question: A classifier maps sensor readings straight to a decision through a single trainable stage of threshold units. It handles most of the task, then stalls on one requirement: two input patterns that share almost none of their active bits must yield the same decision, while patterns sitting between them must yield the other. Adding labelled examples, training far longer, and restarting from new random seeds all leave it at chance on that requirement. What is the diagnosis?
choices: The stage is too narrow rather than too shallow. A sufficiently wide layer of nonlinear units is a universal approximator, so widening the trainable stage until it can carve the region is the principled fix, and the plateau is evidence the width has not yet been reached

The failure is in optimisation, not representation: threshold units are nonlinear, so the capacity to express this mapping exists in the current architecture and gradient descent is stalling in a bad basin. Momentum, a learning-rate schedule, and many more restarts are the appropriate response

This is XOR's shape, and it is a limit of representation that no amount of data, time, or restarts can move. A network whose only trained stage runs input straight to output can only make similar inputs give similar outputs — and similarity here means overlap in the input encoding, which the outside world fixes, not the network. The escape is to change what the network sees: supply the derived conjunction feature by hand, or add a hidden layer that learns such a recoding, which is always guaranteed to exist

The output stage is the bottleneck: a single decision unit is being asked to represent a non-contiguous class. Allocating one output unit per class and training them one-vs-rest gives each unit a simpler region to separate and resolves the requirement without touching the input side
explanation: The engineering skill here is telling a representation problem from an optimisation problem, because the two respond to completely different interventions and only one of them is worth spending a week on. The tell is in the requirement itself: the least-overlapping patterns must share an answer, which is precisely the shape of XOR, where 00 and 11 demand the same output. A one-stage learner has a single essential character — similar inputs produce similar outputs — and the similarity metric is not a hyperparameter, it is the input encoding handed to the network by the world. Once the requirement runs against that character, no quantity of examples or epochs helps, which is exactly the observation the team already made and misread as slow convergence. Minsky and Papert's 1969 analysis is the formal version of this: a map of which mappings these learners can and cannot do, with a long cannot-list. The remedy is to change the representation, and there are two routes: hand the network a feature it lacks, such as "both inputs on", which makes XOR immediately solvable; or add hidden units and let the network invent the recoding, since some internal representation that makes the mapping learnable always exists. The first option is the sharpest distractor because universal approximation is a real theorem being cited from the wrong side — the property belongs to networks with a hidden layer, and width in the single trained stage buys more separating surfaces over the same fixed input similarities. The second option correctly notes that threshold units are nonlinear, which is true and irrelevant: a per-unit nonlinearity on the final stage does not recode the inputs, and the reported symptom — identical failure across many seeds — is itself evidence against a basin-of-attraction story. The fourth option restructures the output, but the missing structure is upstream of the outputs; each one-vs-rest unit inherits the same input similarities and the same limit.

question: Modernising a legacy network of hard-threshold units, a colleague proposes training the hidden layers by "running the perceptron rule backwards" — computing (t − o) at the outputs and pushing it back through the weights — and keeping the threshold activation, on the grounds that it is cheap and is what the perceptron used. What actually blocks this, and what did the 1986 generalized delta rule change?
choices: The obstacle is architectural rather than analytical. In the perceptron the first stage is fixed by construction, so backward signals have nowhere to go; 1986's contribution is making that stage trainable and connecting the layers end to end, which works with threshold activations left unchanged

The perceptron's rule needs a target at every unit it trains, and a hidden unit has none — that is the credit-assignment gap that stood open from 1969. Backprop closes it by making the error a differentiable function of every weight: replace the hard threshold with the logistic squashing function, define E as summed squared error, and gradient descent yields Δw = η·δ·o everywhere, with δⱼ = (tⱼ − oⱼ)·f′(netⱼ) at the outputs and δⱼ = f′(netⱼ)·Σₖ δₖ·wₖⱼ at hidden units — a unit's error signal assembled from the error signals of the units it feeds, through the very weights it sent its output along. Keeping the threshold defeats this, since f′ is zero wherever it is defined and every δ collapses to zero

The quantity is wrong, not the activation. Raw (t − o) must not be sent backwards undivided; the correct backward signal splits the error evenly among the units that contributed to it, and it is that credit-splitting scheme — which needs no derivative and works with thresholds — that 1986 introduced

Nothing blocks it in principle, but the scheme oscillates: with thresholds the updates are all-or-nothing and successive passes undo each other. The 1986 contribution is the momentum term α, which averages those swings and is what makes multi-layer training with threshold units converge
explanation: This tests reading a change of activation function as an enabling architectural decision rather than a detail of numerics. The 1969 wall was never that people lacked the idea of hidden units — the escape was already known — it was that nobody could say how much a hidden unit was to blame for an error it never received a target for. Framing E as a differentiable function of the weights converts that unanswerable question into a derivative, and the recursion is where the answer lives: a hidden unit's δ is the δ of every unit it feeds, weighted by the same connections used on the forward pass, so blame flows back along exactly the paths that carried influence forward. Differentiability is the price of admission, and the hard threshold cannot pay it: its derivative is zero on both flats and undefined at the step, so the f′(netⱼ) factor annihilates every error signal before it reaches the first hidden layer. That is why the logistic squashing function appears — not because it recognises better than a threshold, but because it is what makes credit assignment computable, with Δw = η·δ·o then reading uniformly as error signal of the receiver times output of the sender at every weight in the network. The first option misremembers which stage is fixed and mislocates the difficulty: the perceptron's random S→A wiring is indeed fixed, but the missing piece was a learning rule for units without targets, not permission to connect layers, and freeing a layer without a rule for it changes nothing. The third option invents a derivative-free credit split — the appeal being that it sounds like it would sidestep the activation problem — but even credit-splitting must know how sensitively the error responds to a unit's output, which is what the derivative supplies; an even split ignores the weights entirely and would move units that had no influence. The fourth option promotes a genuine accessory to the headline: momentum is real and is used, but it damps the trajectory of an existing gradient signal, and with thresholds there is no gradient signal to damp.

question: Aiming for reproducible runs, an engineer initialises every weight in a three-layer network to one constant — first 0, then 0.5. Forward passes and loss are computed correctly, and with 0.5 the gradients are non-zero, yet in both runs the hidden units remain indistinguishable from one another and the network never outperforms a single-stage learner, however long it trains. What is going on?
choices: The units are saturated: identical weights of that size drive net inputs into the flat tails of the logistic function where f′ is near zero, so error signals vanish before they reach the hidden layer. Scaling every weight down by a common factor — keeping them identical, which preserves the reproducibility the engineer wants — restores the gradient and the layer trains

Zero initialisation is genuinely fatal, but 0.5 is a different case and does train, since non-zero identical weights produce non-zero gradients and therefore non-zero updates. The stall in the second run points at an unrelated cause such as the learning rate, and the two runs should be diagnosed separately

This is the local-minimum risk the 1986 authors flagged: a perfectly symmetric starting point is the worst basin in the error surface, and gradient descent has no guarantee of escaping it. Restarting from a different constant moves the network into a better basin and lets the hidden layer differentiate

Identical weights make the hidden units identical functions of the input, so they compute the same output, receive the same δ, and take the same update — they remain identical forever. The layer has many units but one degree of freedom, which is exactly why it performs like a network with no hidden layer at all. Backprop's requirement is that weights start small and random: random to break the symmetry so units can specialise into different internal representations, small to keep them in the responsive region of the squashing function. Reproducibility comes from fixing the seed, not from making the values equal
explanation: The reasoning being tested is that a hidden layer's value comes from its units differing, and that an initialisation choice can silently destroy that while leaving every other part of the system working. Symmetry breaking is a structural requirement, not a numerical nicety: backprop updates a weight by η·δ·o, so two units fed by the same inputs with the same weights produce the same o, are handed the same δ from the units they feed, and move by the same Δw on every step. Sameness is a fixed point of the update rule, and no learning rate, schedule, or epoch count is a symmetry-breaking mechanism. The observable symptom follows exactly — a layer of N identical units spans what one unit spans, so the network reduces to a single-stage learner and inherits its ceiling, which is the wall this whole line of work exists to get past. The stated goal is worth separating from the mistake: reproducibility is a legitimate requirement, and a fixed pseudo-random seed delivers it exactly, giving identical runs with non-identical weights. The second option isolates the useful half-truth — zero and 0.5 really do differ in whether gradients vanish — while missing that non-zero updates applied equally to equal weights keep them equal, so the two runs fail for the same reason and diagnosing them separately wastes the effort. The first option raises saturation, which is the real reason initial weights should be small, and then keeps the property that actually causes the failure; shrinking identical weights produces smaller identical updates. The third option reaches for local minima, and it is worth remembering how the 1986 authors characterised those: across hundreds of problems genuine local minima proved very rare, so it is a poor first hypothesis in general — and this is not one, since a symmetric start is not a basin the network is trapped in by the error surface but a subspace the update rule can never leave.

question: In a design review, a colleague dismisses the 1958 perceptron as a dead end with nothing in common with the feedforward blocks in a modern transformer, and argues that only the 1986 paper belongs in the lineage. How do the two papers actually divide the inheritance?
choices: 1958 contributes the shape and 1986 the training, and both are visible in the transformer's position-wise FFN — a two-layer feedforward network trained by backprop, sitting inside every block. Rosenblatt fixes the form: layers of units computing a weighted sum, all connections running forward, learning residing in the connections themselves, memory distributed across them. Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams replace two specifics inside that form — the hard threshold becomes a differentiable activation, and reinforcement-driven value updates become error gradients that reach hidden layers — leaving the shape standing

The colleague has it backwards but the correction is narrower than it looks: none of the 1958 architecture persists, since modern blocks are not stacks of threshold units, while the reinforcement-style value update does survive — as the momentum term in the modern optimizer, which accumulates a running credit for directions that keep being rewarded

Both papers contribute learning rules only. The shape of modern networks traces to the 1969 analysis, which identified the hidden layer as the fix and specified the layered form now in use, leaving just the training rule open for 1986 to supply

1958's surviving contribution is the random fixed projection, which reappears as the transformer's positional encoding and as random weight initialisation; everything trainable in a modern block descends from 1986, so the perceptron's place in the lineage is real but confined to the parts that are never trained
explanation: The judgment here is separating an architecture's form from its training procedure — two things that get bundled together as "the model" and that have independent histories. Split cleanly: 1958 gives the shape, 1986 gives the training. Everything the transformer's position-wise FFN does structurally is Rosenblatt's — units taking a weighted sum of their inputs, arranged in layers with signals running forward, knowledge held in the connection strengths rather than in a separate store, and no unit that can be pointed to as holding a particular fact. What 1986 changed sits inside that unchanged form: differentiable units in place of hard thresholds, and an error signal that propagates back through hidden layers in place of value updates driven by reinforcement without any computed error. That is also why the feed-forward NNLM that later work measures itself against — projection layer, nonlinear hidden layer, softmax output, trained end to end — is recognisably the same machine. The second option correctly rejects the dismissal, then trades one wrong claim for another: threshold units were replaced, but replacing an activation function is not replacing an architecture, and momentum is a smoothing term over successive gradients from the 1986 rule, not a descendant of reinforcement-driven value accumulation. The third option gives 1969 credit it did not claim; that work was an analysis of what one-stage learners cannot do, and while hidden units were named as the escape, the layered form predates it and the open problem it left was precisely the learning rule. The fourth option keeps only the part of the perceptron that does not learn, which inverts the paper's own emphasis — the random wiring is a modelling assumption about imperfect nervous tissue, while the claim that matters, and the one still in force, is that learning lives in the connections.
